policy: All included claims are under review and internal only. Catalog presence, schema validity, citation presence, and automated validation do not establish scientific quality. No entry may be rendered in a reading until a qualified review records scope, status, permitted use, reviewer role, and review date.

claims.claimText: Cortisol can be measured in blood, urine, or saliva, and collection time and protocol are part of interpreting a result; cortisol testing may use multiple samples or a timed urine collection depending on the clinical question.

scope.description: Named cortisol laboratory tests and their collection procedures.
scope.setting: Clinical laboratory or clinician-directed home sampling.
scope.timeframe: At the specified collection time or interval.

limitations: This is a candidate summary of an official patient reference, not an independent evidence review.
It does not define a sampling protocol, reference range, diagnosis, or interpretation for an individual result.
It does not imply that Metheus currently imports or interprets cortisol assays.

claims.claimText: Basal body temperature charting is retrospective for ovulation timing: a temperature rise may indicate that ovulation has already occurred, but BBT alone cannot predict the upcoming ovulation event.

scope.description: Basal body temperature used as one fertility-awareness sign.
scope.population: People using BBT charting in menstrual cycles.
scope.setting: Daily morning temperature tracking under the described method.
scope.outcome: Retrospective indication of an ovulatory transition.

sourceCitations.title: Fertility Awareness-Based Methods of Family Planning

limitations: This candidate describes a particular sign and does not estimate an individual's phase or fertility.
Illness and other conditions can affect temperature interpretation.
This is not contraceptive, fertility, or medical advice.

claims.claimText: Clinical actigraphy estimates selected sleep parameters over time; polysomnography measures sleep-related physiological signals and is used as a reference method. Findings about clinical actigraphy should not be transferred automatically to a consumer wearable algorithm.

scope.description: Clinical actigraphy for evaluation of sleep disorders and circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders.
scope.population: Adult and pediatric patients within the guideline's clinical scope.
scope.setting: Clinical evaluation using actigraphy and related sleep assessment.
scope.comparator: Polysomnography and sleep logs, as relevant to the parameter.
scope.timeframe: Repeated monitoring over the study interval.

sourceCitations.title: Use of Actigraphy for the Evaluation of Sleep Disorders and Circadian Rhythm Sleep-Wake Disorders: An American Academy of Sleep Medicine Clinical Practice Guideline

limitations: The guideline explicitly excludes consumer-marketed wearable devices from its scope.
This statement does not establish the accuracy of a specific device, algorithm, population, or metric.
This is a candidate summary and has not been reviewed for Metheus use.

claims.claimText: Commercial urinary LH tests can identify a midcycle luteinizing-hormone surge that typically precedes ovulation by roughly one to two days; detecting a surge is not identical to directly observing follicular rupture or proving conception.

scope.description: Urinary LH ovulation-predictor tests used during fertility evaluation.
scope.population: People undergoing fertility evaluation, within the cited committee opinion's scope.
scope.outcome: Detection of an LH surge preceding expected ovulation.
scope.timeframe: Approximately one to two days before expected ovulation.

sourceCitations.title: Fertility evaluation of infertile women: a committee opinion

limitations: The cited source is a professional committee opinion; the statement has not received independent Metheus review.
Test performance and interpretation depend on product, timing, user instructions, and clinical context.
This candidate must not be used to estimate an individual's fertility or guide a reproductive decision.

claims.claimText: In one randomized laboratory speech-task study of healthy undergraduates, social-evaluative threat produced greater cortisol and cardiovascular responses than a matched non-evaluative condition; this supports a bounded general mechanism, not an individual-level prediction.

scope.description: Acute social-evaluative threat during a laboratory speech task.
scope.exposureOrSignal: Presence versus absence of evaluators; salivary cortisol and cardiovascular measures.
scope.timeframe: Before, during, and after one stressor.

sourceCitations.title: Social-evaluative threat, cognitive load, and the cortisol and cardiovascular stress response

limitations: Single bounded laboratory task and sample.
Does not establish a fixed appraisal-to-hormone sequence or predict an individual's response.
Does not make cortisol a general stress score or establish effects of ordinary social interactions.

claims.claimText: In an experimental problem-discussion study with young women, observed co-rumination was associated with increased salivary cortisol after accounting for baseline cortisol; this narrow finding should not be generalized to ordinary venting or supportive conversation.

scope.description: Observed co-rumination during a problem discussion between young women.
scope.population: Young women in the study sample.

sourceCitations.title: Co-ruminating increases stress hormone levels in women

limitations: A bounded study does not establish causality for all forms of social disclosure.
Does not imply that venting is generally harmful, that all friends co-ruminate, or that cortisol indexes subjective distress.
Do not infer co-rumination from a record that only says a person talked with a friend.

claims.claimText: A systematic review and meta-analysis of studies in healthy participants found associations between perseverative cognition (including rumination and worry) and cortisol, heart-rate, HRV, and blood-pressure measures; results varied by study design, measurement, and moderators, so they do not establish a universal response or individual prediction.

scope.description: Physiological correlates of experimentally induced or measured perseverative cognition.
scope.population: Healthy participants in the included studies.
scope.setting: Experimental and correlational research represented in a 60-study systematic review and meta-analysis.
scope.exposureOrSignal: Perseverative cognition, including rumination and worry; cortisol, heart rate, HRV, and blood pressure measures.
scope.outcome: Study-level associations with cardiovascular, autonomic, and endocrine measures.
scope.timeframe: Acute laboratory responses and correlational measurement windows, as defined in the included studies.

sourceCitations.title: Physiological concomitants of perseverative cognition: A systematic review and meta-analysis
State rumination links major life stressors to acute stressor cortisol response in healthy adults

limitations: The meta-analysis combined different forms and measures of perseverative cognition and multiple physiological outcomes; moderators included sex, ethnicity, induction, state versus trait measurement, duration, and study quality.
Associations do not establish that rumination caused a physiological response or that a physiological signal reveals rumination.

The 2024 study examined a laboratory social-evaluative stress task in healthy adults; its mediation results differed between cortisol responders and non-responders and do not support a general individual prediction.
Neither source supports inferring an individual's cortisol, HRV, cardiovascular state, diagnosis, or health risk from self-reported rumination.

claims.claimText: In one randomized study, guided expressive writing did not show a general effect on cortisol or HRV reactivity or recovery; an interaction suggested greater cortisol recovery for participants reporting more taxing nominated stressors.

scope.description: Three sessions of expressive writing, guided to encourage constructive emotional processing, compared with unguided writing.
scope.population: Adults writing about a self-nominated stressor (N=151).
scope.setting: Randomized writing intervention followed by a stress-recall task.
scope.exposureOrSignal: Guided versus unguided expressive writing; salivary cortisol and HRV.
scope.timeframe: Writing over three days; stress task two weeks later.

sourceCitations.title: Emotional processing writing and physiological stress responses: understanding constructive and unconstructive processes

limitations: One study does not establish efficacy for journaling generally.
The interaction requires replication and does not support an individual recommendation.
No general cortisol or HRV effect was observed in this sample.

claims.claimText: In one three-week randomized trial of a structured chatbot program for stress, mindfulness, and interoception, the study found no significant change in perceived or momentary stress; mindfulness and reappraisal increased in the intervention group over time. Cortisol was not measured.

scope.description: A structured chatbot-guided psychoeducation and skills program, not an unrestricted conversational AI companion.
scope.population: Adults with medium to high stress levels in a multicenter trial (N=118).
scope.setting: Three-week smartphone intervention with two daily interactive sessions, compared with treatment as usual.
scope.exposureOrSignal: Chatbot-guided content on stress, mindfulness, and interoception.
scope.outcome: Perceived and momentary stress, mindfulness, interoceptive sensibility, well-being, and emotion-regulation measures.
scope.timeframe: Preintervention, after three weeks, and six-week follow-up.

sourceCitations.title: Effects of a Chatbot-Based Intervention on Stress and Health-Related Parameters in a Stressed Sample: Randomized Controlled Trial

limitations: This claim describes one structured program and does not generalize to journaling, venting, a general-purpose chatbot, or other AI systems.
No significant perceived-stress change was observed in this study; within-group increases in mindfulness and reappraisal do not establish a biological mechanism.
Cortisol and other endocrine biomarkers were not measured, so the trial does not support a hormone-response claim.
The candidate has not completed Metheus evidence review and is not eligible for readings.
